title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about making revision work and performing well on the day. You already know why exams matter and how to plan your revision time. The step that separates adequate preparation from strong preparation is what you do with that time: whether you read over material passively, or work with it actively so that it stays with you.

By the end you will be able to evaluate why active revision outperforms passive revision, select and justify active techniques across three categories, and devise an exam-day strategy that protects your performance under pressure.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: evaluate why active revision outperforms passive revision and justify an active-learning approach
select and justify active revision techniques across the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic categories
devise an exam-day strategy that manages time and anxiety to maximise your performance.

title: In real academic practice
body: Active revision and exam performance are not abstract study skills: they decide the grade your knowledge actually earns. Every exam you sit rewards the same things - knowledge you can retrieve under pressure, time you have controlled, and nerves you have managed. The techniques in this course are the ones strong students use to turn preparation into marks, in any subject.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, active learning in revision: why working with knowledge beats reading over it. Second, the active techniques themselves, grouped as visual, auditory and kinaesthetic. Third, exam-day strategy: how to turn preparation into performance under exam conditions. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You have planned your revision and worked out where your gaps are. Now comes the question that decides how much of that effort pays off: what do you actually do in a revision session? This lesson is about the difference between revision that reads over material and revision that works with it, and why the second kind deepens knowledge.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are not just being shown techniques to copy. You are expected to judge why active revision works, to pick approaches with reasons, and to defend the choices you make. The aim is a revision programme you can justify, not a checklist you follow.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: evaluate active against passive revision and justify why active engagement deepens knowledge and understanding
analyse a worked example to identify what makes a revision approach active rather than passive
justify an active-learning move you would use on a revision task in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Passive revision takes knowledge in: you read a textbook, review your notes, and hope that exposure is enough. Active revision does something with that knowledge: you reproduce it, test yourself on it, and rebuild it in a new form. The reading may look similar; the learning is not, because producing knowledge forces a depth of processing that re-reading never reaches.

This is why active learning is the principle behind every technique in this course. Each technique is a different way of making yourself retrieve, reorganise or explain what you know. Switching between them also sustains cognitive resilience: the capacity to stay focused and effective across a long revision period.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think back to your last revision session. Judge how much of it was active rather than passive, and justify one change that would make the next session work harder.

title: Summary
body: Active revision is not more time with your books; it is a different kind of work with them. You can now contrast active and passive revision and explain why producing and testing knowledge deepens it, and you can analyse an approach to judge whether it is truly active. The next lesson turns this principle into the specific techniques you can choose from.

title: Orientation
body: Active learning is the principle; techniques are how you put it to work. This lesson sets out the main active revision techniques, grouped into three families: visual, auditory and kinaesthetic. The point is not to use all of them, but to choose well, and to combine techniques from more than one family so your revision stays varied and effective.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not being asked to memorise a list of techniques. You are expected to weigh what each one is good for, judge which turn a passive task into an active one, and build a mix that suits the topic in front of you. The reasoning behind your choices matters as much as the choices themselves.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: distinguish visual, auditory and kinaesthetic revision techniques and what each is suited to
evaluate which techniques turn a passive revision task into an active one
combine active techniques from more than one category and defend the mix for a topic in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Active revision techniques fall into three families. Visual techniques - mind maps, visual notes, flashcards, mnemonics, posters - turn knowledge into images, patterns and spatial layouts you can picture under pressure. Auditory techniques - reading aloud, audio recordings, discussion groups - use speaking and listening to process and recall ideas. Kinaesthetic techniques - spatial placing, role-play, movement, interactive models - use physical action and place to anchor what you know.

What makes any of them work is not the family it belongs to, but whether it makes you produce knowledge rather than receive it. The strongest revision draws on more than one family, because variety both deepens understanding and sustains the focus a long revision period demands.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Which of the three families - visual, auditory, kinaesthetic - do you rely on, and which do you neglect? Make the case for a more balanced mix on your next topic.

title: Summary
body: Active revision techniques come in three families: visual, auditory and kinaesthetic. You can now distinguish them and say what each suits, evaluate which ones turn a passive task active, and select a mix across families for a given topic. What unites the strong choices is production: making yourself rebuild, explain or enact knowledge rather than merely review it. The final lesson takes your prepared knowledge into the exam itself.

title: Orientation
body: Strong revision can still be wasted by a poor hour in the exam hall. This lesson is about exam-day strategy: the decisions, before and during the exam, that turn your preparation into marks. Much of it is about managing time and nerves, because both can undo knowledge you genuinely have.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not being handed a set of rules to obey. You are expected to see why each decision protects your performance, to read contrasting approaches and judge what works, and to build a plan you could defend for an exam of your own. A strategy you understand is one you can adapt when an exam surprises you.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain how an organised exam-day approach manages anxiety and protects performance
analyse contrasting exam-day approaches to identify the decisions that maximise performance
devise an exam-day plan, including timing, for an exam in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Exam-day strategy begins before the exam does. Arriving in good time, bringing everything you need, and settling your nerves all remove distractions that would otherwise eat into your thinking. Once the exam starts, the strategy is mostly about time. You read the instructions, work out how long each section deserves, plan briefly before you write, and watch the clock so no single answer swallows the time meant for another.

None of this is about knowing more. It is about protecting the knowledge you already have from the two things that waste it most: panic and poor timekeeping. A clear plan, made in advance and adjusted as the exam unfolds, is what lets your preparation show.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Recall your last exam. Where did time or nerves cost you marks, and justify the one change to your exam-day plan that would protect your performance most?

title: Summary
body: Exam-day strategy is how prepared knowledge becomes marks. You can now explain how an organised approach manages anxiety and protects performance, analyse contrasting approaches to spot the decisions that matter, and devise a timed plan for an exam of your own. With active revision behind you and a clear plan for the day, your preparation has the best chance to show.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Revision is no longer just time spent with your books: it is active work you can justify. You can evaluate why active revision outperforms passive, because producing and testing knowledge processes it more deeply than reading does. You can select techniques across the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic families, and say why each suits the material. And you can devise an exam-day strategy that controls time and settles nerves so your preparation shows. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, active revision and a clear exam-day plan are habits you carry into every exam you sit. Each topic you rebuild rather than reread, each technique you choose with a reason, each paper you pace to the clock, is this approach at work. The same discipline - producing knowledge, managing time, staying calm under pressure - also travels into the deadlines and high-stakes moments of professional life.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The active revision cycle
body: Active revision is a cycle, not a single read. Work through the four stages to see how one topic is turned from pages into knowledge you can retrieve.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal what it involves. Work through all four.

_items.title: Read with a purpose
_items.body: You read the source once, not to absorb it whole, but to find the few ideas worth the effort of revising. Reading is where active revision starts, not where it ends.

_items.title: Reproduce it
_items.body: You close the book and rebuild the idea from memory, as a diagram, a summary or a spoken explanation. Reproducing forces you to notice what you cannot yet recall.

_items.title: Test and check
_items.body: You test yourself on the gaps that reproducing exposed, then return to the source only to settle what you got wrong. The test, not the text, drives the next round.

_items.title: Vary and sustain
_items.body: You switch technique and topic to keep your attention fresh. Variety is not decoration: it protects the cognitive resilience a long revision period demands.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Three families of technique
body: The active techniques group into three families. Open each to see what it contains and what it suits, then see how the families combine.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Visual
_items.body: Mind maps, visual notes, flashcards, mnemonics and posters turn knowledge into images and spatial patterns. A mind map forces you to show how ideas connect; a flashcard makes you retrieve an answer rather than recognise it. These suit material with structure, relationships or processes you can lay out and see.

_items.title: Auditory
_items.body: Reading aloud, recording yourself and discussing ideas in a group use speech to process knowledge. Explaining a theory aloud exposes the points you cannot yet put into words, and a recording lets you revise during time that would otherwise be lost. These suit ideas you need to articulate precisely.

_items.title: Kinaesthetic
_items.body: Spatial placing, role-play, physical movement and interactive models anchor knowledge in action and place. Walking while you rehearse, or putting concept cards in different rooms, ties recall to a physical trigger. These suit procedures, sequences and practice-based knowledge you learn by doing.

_items.title: Mixing the families
_items.body: The strongest revision combines families rather than staying in one. You might map a topic visually, explain it aloud, then test yourself while walking. Variety deepens understanding and keeps your attention fresh, which is what sustains cognitive resilience across weeks of revision.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Decisions that protect your marks
body: Exam-day strategy is a set of decisions, before and during the exam. Review each card to see what it protects.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Arrive settled
_items.subtitle: Before the exam
_items.text: Get there early with everything you need: spare pens, a watch, water. Removing small worries protects your attention for the exam itself.

_items.title: Read before you write
_items.subtitle: First minutes
_items.text: Read the instructions and every question before choosing. Knowing what the paper asks stops you answering the wrong question well.

_items.title: Plan your time
_items.subtitle: Throughout
_items.text: Divide the time by the marks, note when each answer must end, and plan briefly before writing. Timing stops one answer stealing another's marks.

_items.title: Write to time
_items.subtitle: Under pressure
_items.text: Watch the clock and be disciplined enough to finish an answer even when it is not perfect. A finished paper beats a brilliant half.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students set aside the same number of hours to revise the same topic.

{{learner-a}} spends the time reading. The textbook chapter is read once, then again, and key passages are highlighted. It feels like steady progress, and by the end {{learner-a}} has covered every page. But nothing has been produced: no diagram, no self-test, no explanation in their own words. When a past question comes up later, the material feels familiar yet strangely hard to reproduce. This is passive revision.

{{learner-b}} reads the same chapter once, then closes it. The ideas are rebuilt from memory as a mind map, gaps are turned into test questions, and the hardest concept is explained aloud and recorded. Each gap that surfaces sends {{learner-b}} back to the text with a purpose. By the end the topic can be retrieved, not just recognised. This is active revision.

Both students spent the same hours. Only {{learner-b}} turned those hours into knowledge that would survive the exam, by producing and testing rather than only reading.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students need to revise the same difficult theory, one with several linked stages.

{{learner-a}} makes a single set of neat written notes and reads them over each day. The notes are accurate and the method is tidy, but it never leaves one family: everything is reading. The stages blur together, because nothing forces {{learner-a}} to reproduce the sequence or say it aloud. One passive technique, repeated, is still passive.

{{learner-b}} draws the theory as a flow diagram, then explains each stage aloud into a recording, then walks through the stages physically in order. Three techniques from three families, each demanding a different kind of production. The visual map fixes the structure, the spoken version catches the gaps, and the movement anchors the sequence. This is a varied, active approach.

Both revised the same theory for the same time. {{learner-b}} chose techniques across families that matched the material, and ended with knowledge that could be retrieved by more than one route.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students, equally well revised, sit the same two-hour exam.

{{learner-a}} arrives just in time and hurries to the desk, flustered. With only one pen and no watch, {{learner-a}} scans the paper, spots a familiar keyword, and writes everything known about it. That answer takes over an hour, which leaves too little time for the second question, half understood and rushed. The knowledge was there; the strategy let it leak away.

{{learner-b}} arrives early, lays out pens and a watch, and reads the instructions before anything else. Seeing that two questions carry equal marks, {{learner-b}} allots an hour each, spends ten minutes planning, and writes to that plan. When time runs short on the second answer, {{learner-b}} wraps it up with a brief conclusion rather than leaving it unfinished. The preparation showed because the time was controlled.

Both knew the material. Only {{learner-b}} protected that knowledge with timing and a calm start, and so turned it into a complete paper.

title: Practical guidance
displayTitle: Is this revision active?
body: Use these questions to check that your approach is genuinely active, and that you can defend it.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it against your own revision.

_items.text: Have I closed the source and rebuilt the idea from memory, rather than only re-reading it?
Have I turned each gap I found into a question to test myself on?
Have I produced something, a diagram, a summary or a recording, that I can check against the source?
Have I returned to the text with a specific purpose, rather than reading it start to finish again?
Have I varied my techniques and topics to keep my attention and resilience up?
Can I justify why each technique I chose suits the material I am revising?

title: Practical guidance
displayTitle: Building a varied technique mix
body: Use these questions to check that your approach is genuinely active, and that you can defend it.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it against your own revision.

_items.text: Have I identified what kind of material this is, such as structure, argument or procedure, before choosing a technique?
Have I chosen at least one technique that makes me produce the knowledge, not just review it?
Have I drawn on more than one family: visual, auditory or kinaesthetic?
Can I say why each technique suits this particular topic?
Have I used a technique that exposes my gaps, rather than hiding them?
Does my mix vary enough to hold my attention across a long session?

title: Practical guidance
displayTitle: Your exam-day plan
body: Use these questions to check that your approach is genuinely active, and that you can defend it.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it against your own revision.

_items.text: Have I planned to arrive early, with spare pens and a watch?
Will I read the instructions and all the questions before I start writing?
Have I worked out how to divide the time according to the marks?
Have I set a point at which each answer must end?
Do I plan briefly before writing each answer, rather than starting cold?
Am I prepared to finish a weaker answer rather than abandon it unfinished?

title: Formative check: why active revision works
displayTitle: Which of these best explains why active revision deepens knowledge more than passive revision?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does active revision deepen knowledge more than passive revision?

_items.text: Producing and testing knowledge forces a deeper level of processing than re-reading does.
_items.feedback: Yes. Rebuilding and testing knowledge is what makes it stick.

_items.text: It involves spending more total hours with the material.
_items.feedback: Time alone is not the point; passive revision can take just as long.

_items.text: It means reading the source more carefully and more often.
_items.feedback: Careful re-reading is still passive; nothing is produced or tested.

_items.text: It relies on highlighting the most important passages.
_items.feedback: Highlighting marks the text but does not make you retrieve it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Producing and testing knowledge processes it more deeply than reading ever can.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about producing and testing, rather than reading more.
_incorrect.final: Active revision works because producing and testing knowledge processes it deeply. More hours, more careful reading and highlighting are all still passive.

title: Formative check: analysing the example
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's revision active rather than passive?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's revision active?

_items.text: They rebuilt the material from memory and tested themselves, returning to the text only to fix gaps.
_items.feedback: Yes. Producing and testing, then targeting the text, is active revision.

_items.text: They spent more hours revising than the first student.
_items.feedback: Both spent the same time; the difference was what they did with it.

_items.text: They read the chapter more carefully than the first student.
_items.feedback: Careful reading is still passive; the second student produced and tested.

_items.text: They highlighted the most important passages in the textbook.
_items.feedback: The first student highlighted; it did not make their revision active.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Rebuilding from memory and testing, then returning to the text with purpose, is what made it active.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student DID with the material, beyond reading it.
_incorrect.final: The second student rebuilt the material from memory and tested themselves, returning to the text only to fix gaps. Extra hours, careful reading and highlighting are all still passive.

title: Formative check: justifying a move
displayTitle: You are revising a demanding topic in {{context}}. Which move best shows the active-learning approach this lesson argues for?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move best shows the active-learning approach in your subject?

_items.text: Rebuild the topic from memory in your own form, then test yourself on what you could not recall.
_items.feedback: Yes. Producing and testing is the active move, whatever the subject.

_items.text: Read the key chapter twice, slowly and carefully.
_items.feedback: Careful re-reading is passive; it does not make you produce the knowledge.

_items.text: Copy the main points into neat, well-organised notes.
_items.feedback: Copying organises the text but does not test your recall.

_items.text: Highlight the passages that look most likely to come up.
_items.feedback: Highlighting marks the text; it does not deepen or test your knowledge.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, rebuilding from memory and testing yourself is the active-learning move.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that makes you produce and test the knowledge.
_incorrect.final: The active move in {{context}} is to rebuild the topic from memory and test yourself. Re-reading, copying and highlighting all leave the knowledge unproduced.

title: Formative check: the three families
displayTitle: Which statement best distinguishes the three families of active revision techniques?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement best distinguishes the three families of techniques?

_items.text: Visual uses images and layout, auditory uses speech and listening, and kinaesthetic uses movement and place.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is exactly what separates the three families.

_items.text: Visual is for science, auditory is for languages, and kinaesthetic is for sport.
_items.feedback: The families are defined by how you engage, not by subject.

_items.text: Visual is the most effective, auditory the next, and kinaesthetic the least.
_items.feedback: No family is inherently best; it depends on the material and on you.

_items.text: Visual is active, while auditory and kinaesthetic are passive.
_items.feedback: All three can be active; what matters is whether you produce knowledge.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The families differ by how you engage: images, speech or movement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about how you engage, not about subjects or ranking.
_incorrect.final: The families differ by how you engage: visual uses images and layout, auditory uses speech and listening, kinaesthetic uses movement and place. They are not tied to subjects or ranked by worth.

title: Formative check: evaluating the example
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's revision more active than the first student's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's revision more active?

_items.text: They used techniques from several families, each forcing them to produce the knowledge in a different way.
_items.feedback: Yes. Varied production across families is what made it active.

_items.text: They made neater and more accurate notes than the first student.
_items.feedback: Neat notes that are only reread stay within one passive technique.

_items.text: They spent longer revising than the first student.
_items.feedback: Both revised for the same time; the difference was the approach.

_items.text: They read their single set of notes more often.
_items.feedback: Re-reading one set of notes is the first student's passive method.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Drawing on several families, each demanding production, is what made it active.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about producing knowledge across more than one family.
_incorrect.final: The second student used techniques from several families, each forcing a different kind of production. Neater notes, more time or more re-reading would all have stayed passive.

title: Formative check: selecting techniques
displayTitle: You are revising a topic in {{context}} that has both a structure to grasp and a procedure to carry out. Which choice best matches this lesson's advice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which choice best matches the advice on combining techniques?

_items.text: Combine a visual technique for the structure with a kinaesthetic one for the procedure.
_items.feedback: Yes. Matching techniques from different families to the material is the advised approach.

_items.text: Choose one technique you like and use it for the whole topic.
_items.feedback: Staying in one family misses the gains of variety across families.

_items.text: Read the relevant notes and chapters several times over.
_items.feedback: Re-reading is passive, whatever the material demands.

_items.text: Make a single detailed set of notes and review it daily.
_items.feedback: One passive technique repeated is still passive.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, matching a visual technique to the structure and a kinaesthetic one to the procedure fits the material.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that draws on more than one family to match the material.
_incorrect.final: The advised choice in {{context}} is to combine families, such as a visual technique for structure and a kinaesthetic one for a procedure. One technique, re-reading or daily review all stay passive or single-family.

title: Formative check: why strategy protects performance
displayTitle: Why does an organised exam-day approach protect your performance?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does an organised exam-day approach protect performance?

_items.text: It removes panic and poor timekeeping, the two things most likely to waste knowledge you already have.
_items.feedback: Yes. Strategy guards prepared knowledge against nerves and lost time.

_items.text: It adds to the amount of knowledge you can recall in the exam.
_items.feedback: Strategy does not add knowledge; it protects what you already have.

_items.text: It guarantees you will finish every question in full.
_items.feedback: No strategy guarantees that; it helps you use the time well.

_items.text: It replaces the need to revise actively beforehand.
_items.feedback: Strategy works with good revision, it does not replace it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An organised approach protects prepared knowledge from panic and poor timekeeping.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what wastes knowledge you already have on the day.
_incorrect.final: An organised approach protects your performance by removing panic and poor timekeeping. It does not add knowledge, guarantee a full paper, or replace revision.

title: Formative check: analysing the example
displayTitle: In the worked example, which decision most clearly cost the first student marks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which decision most clearly cost the first student marks?

_items.text: Spending over an hour on one answer, leaving too little time for the second.
_items.feedback: Yes. Poor timekeeping left the second answer rushed and incomplete.

_items.text: Arriving only a few minutes before the start.
_items.feedback: A late arrival raised the stress, but the lost marks came from timing.

_items.text: Choosing a question with a familiar keyword.
_items.feedback: The problem was not the choice but spending too long on it.

_items.text: Bringing only one pen into the exam.
_items.feedback: One pen is a risk, but it was the timing that cost the marks.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Letting one answer run over an hour left too little time for the other.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the decision about how the time was spent across the two answers.
_incorrect.final: The clearest cost was spending over an hour on one answer, which left too little time for the second. The late arrival and single pen added stress but did not directly lose the marks.

title: Formative check: devising a plan
displayTitle: You are planning for a two-hour exam in {{context}} with two equally weighted questions. Which plan best fits this lesson's strategy?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which plan best fits the exam-day strategy?

_items.text: Allow an hour for each, plan briefly before writing, and set a time to move on.
_items.feedback: Yes. Dividing the time by the marks and holding to it is the strategy.

_items.text: Start with the question you know best and write until you run out of things to say.
_items.feedback: Writing without a time limit risks starving the second answer.

_items.text: Spend the first hour making one answer as complete as possible.
_items.feedback: Perfecting one answer leaves too little time for the other.

_items.text: Read only the question you intend to answer, to save time.
_items.feedback: Skipping the instructions risks answering the wrong question.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, an hour each with brief planning and a firm move-on time fits the strategy.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that divides the time by the marks and holds to it.
_incorrect.final: The sound plan for {{context}} is an hour each, brief planning, and a set time to move on. Writing until you dry up, perfecting one answer, or skipping the instructions all waste time or risk the wrong question.

body: Why does active revision generally produce better exam results than passive revision?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does active revision generally produce better exam results?

_items.text: It makes you produce and test knowledge, which processes it more deeply than re-reading.
_items.feedback: Yes. Production and testing deepen learning.

_items.text: It always takes more hours than passive revision.
_items.feedback: Time is not the reason; it is what you do with it.

_items.text: It lets you avoid the topics you find difficult.
_items.feedback: Active revision targets difficult topics rather than avoiding them.

_items.text: It removes the need to read the source at all.
_items.feedback: Reading still has a place; active revision builds on it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Producing and testing knowledge processes it more deeply than re-reading.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what active revision makes you do with the material.

body: A student rereads their notes several times but never tests themselves or reproduces the material. How is this best described?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How is re-reading without testing best described?

_items.text: Passive revision.
_items.feedback: Yes. Taking knowledge in without producing it is passive.

_items.text: Active revision.
_items.feedback: Active revision would make them reproduce or test the material.

_items.text: Cognitive resilience.
_items.feedback: That is the capacity to stay focused, not a way of revising.

_items.text: Synthesis.
_items.feedback: Synthesis means combining ideas; re-reading does neither.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Re-reading without producing or testing is passive revision.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Did the student produce or test anything, or only take it in?

body: Mind maps, flashcards and posters belong to which family of active revision techniques?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Mind maps, flashcards and posters belong to which family?

_items.text: Visual.
_items.feedback: Yes. These turn knowledge into images and layouts.

_items.text: Auditory.
_items.feedback: Auditory techniques use speech and listening, such as reading aloud.

_items.text: Kinaesthetic.
_items.feedback: Kinaesthetic techniques use movement and place.

_items.text: None: they are passive techniques.
_items.feedback: Made and tested, these are active visual techniques.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Mind maps, flashcards and posters are visual techniques.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whether they use images, speech or movement.

body: What is the main reason for drawing on techniques from more than one family?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why draw on techniques from more than one family?

_items.text: Variety deepens understanding and sustains focus across a long revision period.
_items.feedback: Yes. Variety both deepens learning and protects resilience.

_items.text: It proves to your tutor that you have revised thoroughly.
_items.feedback: The reason is about your learning, not about proof.

_items.text: One family is correct for each subject and must be matched.
_items.feedback: Families are not tied to subjects in that way.

_items.text: It lets you avoid the techniques you find difficult.
_items.feedback: The point is effectiveness, not avoidance.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Variety deepens understanding and sustains focus.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what variety does for your learning and attention.

body: What is the main purpose of an exam-day strategy?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the main purpose of an exam-day strategy?

_items.text: To protect the knowledge you already have from panic and poor timekeeping.
_items.feedback: Yes. Strategy guards prepared knowledge on the day.

_items.text: To make up for revision you did not do.
_items.feedback: Strategy cannot replace revision; it protects its results.

_items.text: To help you recall more facts than you revised.
_items.feedback: It does not add knowledge; it protects what you have.

_items.text: To finish the exam as quickly as possible.
_items.feedback: Speed is not the aim; controlled use of time is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An exam-day strategy protects prepared knowledge from panic and poor timekeeping.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what most often wastes knowledge you already have.

body: In a two-hour exam with two equally weighted questions, what is the soundest use of time?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the soundest use of time in a two-question exam?

_items.text: About an hour on each, with brief planning before writing.
_items.feedback: Yes. Dividing time by the marks protects both answers.

_items.text: Spend as long as it takes to perfect the first answer.
_items.feedback: Perfecting one answer starves the other of time.

_items.text: Write continuously without watching the clock.
_items.feedback: Ignoring the clock is how one answer swallows another's time.

_items.text: Leave the harder question out to save time.
_items.feedback: Both carry equal marks; skipping one forfeits half the paper.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An hour each, with brief planning, divides the time by the marks.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how equal marks should shape the time you give each answer.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: active learning and why it beats passive revision, the visual, auditory and kinaesthetic techniques that put it to work, and an exam-day strategy for the day itself. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one plan.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage the aim is not a perfect routine. It is to see these three as one connected approach rather than three separate lessons, so that it carries on past this course into every exam you sit.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together active learning, a varied technique mix and an exam-day strategy into one connected plan
recognise the three strands working together in a worked example of one student's preparation
plan how you will run active revision and an exam-day strategy together for your {{context}} exams.

title: Concept: definition
body: A connected plan is active revision made whole. Active learning is the principle behind it: you work with knowledge rather than read over it. The visual, auditory and kinaesthetic techniques are how you put that principle to work. The exam-day strategy carries the same deliberate control into the exam itself. The three earlier lessons are the parts of this one plan.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, the plan runs from your first revision session to your last answer. You decide to work with the material actively, choose a varied mix of techniques to suit each topic, and keep testing yourself as you go. Then you carry that same control into the exam with a timed, calm plan. One joined-up approach does far more than three separate efforts.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of your next exam. How will you run active revision, a varied technique mix and an exam-day plan as one connected approach, and when will you start?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Active revision works best as one connected plan, not three separate efforts. You let active learning guide a varied technique mix, run it across your programme, and carry the same control into a timed exam-day plan. It is the joined-up approach, from first session to final answer, that turns preparation into marks.

title: The steps as one process
displayTitle: The steps as one process
body: The earlier lessons come together as one build that runs from a principle to exam day. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Revise actively
_items.body: Decide to revise actively, working with the knowledge rather than reading over it.

_items.title: Choose techniques
_items.body: Choose a varied mix of visual, auditory and kinaesthetic techniques to suit the topic.

_items.title: Run the programme
_items.body: Run that active revision across your programme, testing yourself and carrying gaps back in.

_items.title: Sit the exam
_items.body: Carry the same control into the exam with a timed, calm exam-day plan.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students prepared for the same exam. One revised by reading notes over, used a single technique, and made no plan for the day, then ran out of time in the exam. The other revised actively, mixed visual, auditory and kinaesthetic techniques, and sat the exam to a timed plan. Their preparation held together, and it showed in the result.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to run it as one plan
body: Use these to check your preparation works as one connected plan, not three separate efforts.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Am I working with the knowledge, not just reading over it?
Have I chosen techniques from more than one family to suit the topic?
Am I testing myself and carrying each gap back into the next session?
Does my exam-day plan carry the same control into the exam itself?
Can I justify each choice, from first revision session to final answer?

displayTitle: Why is it better to treat active revision, your technique mix and your exam-day strategy as one connected plan rather than three separate tasks?
body: Why is it better to treat active revision, your technique mix and your exam-day strategy as one connected plan rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it better to treat active revision, your technique mix and your exam-day strategy as one connected plan rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Because each strand feeds the next: the active principle guides your technique choice, and that revision is what your exam-day plan protects.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands support one another when you run them as one plan.

_items.text: Because doing three separate tasks always takes more hours than doing one.
_items.feedback: Time is not the point; one plan is not simply quicker.

_items.text: Because only the exam-day strategy really affects your marks.
_items.feedback: The exam-day plan protects marks, but it protects revision the other two strands built.

_items.text: Because active learning replaces the need for any techniques or exam-day plan.
_items.feedback: Active learning is the principle; the techniques and exam-day plan are how you carry it through.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Run as one plan, the principle guides the techniques, and both are what your exam-day strategy protects.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about the three strands feeding one another.

displayTitle: A student revises a topic actively, uses a mix of techniques across families, and sits the exam to a calm, timed plan. They do better than on earlier exams. What does this show?
body: A student revises a topic actively, uses a mix of techniques across families, and sits the exam to a calm, timed plan. They do better than on earlier exams. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student revises a topic actively, uses a mix of techniques across families, and sits the exam to a calm, timed plan. They do better than on earlier exams. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three strands work together: active revision, a varied technique mix and an exam-day plan form one approach.
_items.feedback: Yes. The strands joined up into one plan, and that is what paid off.

_items.text: That only the exam-day plan made the difference to their result.
_items.feedback: The exam-day plan protected marks, but active revision and the technique mix earned them.

_items.text: That they simply spent far more hours than before.
_items.feedback: The point is the joined-up approach, not extra hours.

_items.text: That the techniques alone, without active learning behind them, improved the result.
_items.feedback: The techniques work because active learning is the principle driving them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three strands ran as one plan, and the result followed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about the three strands working together.

displayTitle: You want to use this approach to prepare for your {{context}} exams this term. Which plan best treats your preparation as one connected whole?
body: You want to use this approach to prepare for your {{context}} exams this term. Which plan best treats your preparation as one connected whole?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this approach to prepare for your your subject exams this term. Which plan best treats your preparation as one connected whole?

_items.text: Revise actively with a varied mix of techniques, then carry the same control into a timed exam-day plan.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three strands as one connected plan.

_items.text: Read your notes over several times, then rely on staying calm on the day.
_items.feedback: Re-reading is passive, and calm alone cannot replace active revision.

_items.text: Pick one favourite technique and use only it, with no exam-day plan.
_items.feedback: One technique and no plan leaves two of the three strands out.

_items.text: Focus only on an exam-day plan and leave revision to the last night.
_items.feedback: An exam-day plan cannot protect revision you have not done.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Active revision, a varied technique mix and a timed exam-day plan make one connected whole.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that runs all three strands together.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Which description best fits active revision run as one connected plan?
body: Which description best fits active revision run as one connected plan?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which description best fits active revision run as one connected plan?

_items.text: Active learning guides a varied technique mix, and a timed exam-day plan protects the result.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Reading your notes over until the exam, then hoping nerves stay calm.
_items.feedback: That is passive revision with no plan.

_items.text: Using a single technique and no exam-day strategy.
_items.feedback: That leaves out two of the three strands.

_items.text: An exam-day plan on its own, with no active revision behind it.
_items.feedback: A plan cannot protect revision you have not done.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student revises actively across families all term, then sits the exam to a calm, timed plan and does better than before. Which parts of the one connected plan did they use?
body: A student revises actively across families all term, then sits the exam to a calm, timed plan and does better than before. Which parts of the one connected plan did they use?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student revises actively across families all term, then sits the exam to a calm, timed plan and does better than before. Which parts of the one connected plan did they use?

_items.text: The active principle, a varied technique mix and an exam-day strategy, run together.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Only the exam-day plan, since nothing before it mattered.
_items.feedback: Active revision and the technique mix built the knowledge the plan protected.

_items.text: Only extra hours spent reading over notes.
_items.feedback: The approach was active and varied, not just more reading.

_items.text: A single technique used on its own.
_items.feedback: They drew on all three strands, not one technique.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
